Mathematical Foundations of the Quadratic-Form Permutation Saddlepoint

Source: vignettes/mathematical-foundations.Rmd
mathematical-foundations.Rmd

This memo explains how fastperm computes the tail probability of a quadratic-form test statistic under a within-stratum permutation null, why each step is built the way it is, and where each decision lives in the code and in the test suite. It is written to be read start to finish: the plain idea first, a small concrete case next, then the notation. Code and test pointers are collected in the final section so the prose stays about the method.

1. The problem, and why one function serves three front ends

A researcher comparing treated and control groups across several covariates wants a single number that says whether the groups are jointly balanced, and a p-value for it that does not assume large samples. The natural statistic is a Mahalanobis-type distance of the treated-group score vector from its permutation mean, Q=(T−μ)′M−1(T−μ),Tc=∑iziscorei,c, Q = (T - \mu)' \, M^{-1} \, (T - \mu), \qquad T_c = \sum_i z_i \, \text{score}_{i,c}, where zz is the 0/1 treatment vector, TT is the vector of treated-group score sums across rr representations (covariates, basis functions, or test statistics), μ=E[T]\mu = E[T] is the exact permutation mean, and MM is a fixed symmetric positive-definite metric. The null is the within-stratum permutation of zz that holds each stratum’s treated count fixed.

Three different tests are the same computation with a different MM:

  • the fastperm omnibus combination uses M=ΣM = \Sigma, a pooled covariance;
  • the RItools balanceTest omnibus d2d^2 of Hansen and Bowers (2008) uses M=VdM = V_d, the permutation covariance of TT, so QQ is asymptotically χrank(Vd)2\chi^2_{\,\mathrm{rank}(V_d)};
  • the RItools covariate-covariance omnibus uses M=ΣxM = \Sigma_x, so QQ is asymptotically a weighted sum of chi-squares.

The point that makes this one function and not three: MM does not change across the permutation. Both VdV_d and Σx\Sigma_x are functions of the covariates and the stratum sizes, not of zz. So MM is a parameter of the computation, supplied by the caller, and the metric is never hard-wired.

2. The rotation reduction: the metric is preprocessing

The first decision removes the metric from the hard part of the problem. For any matrix RR with RR′=M−1R R' = M^{-1} (take R=M−1/2R = M^{-1/2} from the spectral decomposition, dropping numerically-zero eigenvalues so a rank-deficient metric projects onto its range), Q=(T−μ)′M−1(T−μ)=(T−μ)′RR′(T−μ)=‖R′(T−μ)‖2. Q = (T-\mu)' M^{-1} (T-\mu) = (T-\mu)' R R' (T-\mu) = \lVert R'(T-\mu) \rVert^2 . So QQ is a plain sum of squares of the rotated, centred statistic e=R′(T−μ)e = R'(T-\mu). The metric enters only as the one-time rotation; everything downstream works on ee. This is exact, not an approximation: the test suite checks it to machine precision against full enumeration of the permutation orbit.

In rotated coordinates write e=Ty−μye = T_y - \mu_y with Ty=R′TT_y = R'T the rotated statistic and μy=R′μ\mu_y = R'\mu its mean. The eigenvalues λ1,…,λr\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r of the rotated permutation covariance R′VdRR' V_d R are the weights that appear below.

3. The two engines

fastperm_spa_quadratic(scores, treatment, strata, metric, method) offers two inversions of the same statistic.

  • method = "gaussian" (M1) treats ee as Gaussian with the exact permutation covariance. Then QQ is a weighted sum of independent χ12\chi^2_1 variables, Q=∑kλkχ12Q = \sum_k \lambda_k \chi^2_{1}, whose cumulant generating function (CGF) is closed form and inverted by Lugannani-Rice.
  • method = "saddlepoint" (M2) drops the Gaussian assumption and uses the exact permutation CGF of QQ, so the true skewness and higher cumulants of the permutation law enter the tail.

M1 is fast and is the right tool when ee is close to Gaussian (large strata). M2 is the tool when ee is skewed and discrete – few strata, small nn, many covariates – which is exactly where balance testing lives and where the Gaussian tail drifts.

4. M1: the Gaussian weighted-chi-square tail

4.1 The CGF and Lugannani-Rice

For Q=∑kλkχ12Q = \sum_k \lambda_k \chi^2_1 with λk>0\lambda_k > 0 the CGF is K(θ)=−12∑klog⁡(1−2θλk), K(\theta) = -\tfrac12 \sum_k \log(1 - 2\theta\lambda_k), analytic and steep on θ∈(−∞,1/(2λmax))\theta \in (-\infty,\, 1/(2\lambda_{\max})), with a pole at θ=1/(2λmax)\theta = 1/(2\lambda_{\max}). The Lugannani-Rice tail approximation is P(Q≥q)≈1−Φ(ŵ)+ϕ(ŵ)(1û−1ŵ),ŵ=sign⁡(θ̂)2(θ̂q−K(θ̂)),û=θ̂K″(θ̂), P(Q \ge q) \approx 1 - \Phi(\hat w) + \phi(\hat w)\left(\frac{1}{\hat u} - \frac{1}{\hat w}\right), \quad \hat w = \operatorname{sign}(\hat\theta)\sqrt{2(\hat\theta q - K(\hat\theta))}, \quad \hat u = \hat\theta\sqrt{K''(\hat\theta)}, where the saddlepoint θ̂\hat\theta solves K′(θ̂)=qK'(\hat\theta) = q. This reproduces CompQuadForm::imhof (the exact inversion of the same Gaussian-dd distribution) to about 1% relative error in the tail – the saddlepoint’s own accuracy, not slack – and reduces to the χr2\chi^2_r tail when M=VdM = V_d makes all λk=1\lambda_k = 1.

4.2 The near-mean correction

The term 1/û−1/ŵ1/\hat u - 1/\hat w is a removable 0/00/0 at q=E[Q]q = E[Q], where ŵ→0\hat w \to 0 and û→0\hat u \to 0. Worse, the difference loses precision to cancellation (ŵ≈û\hat w \approx \hat u) over a whole neighbourhood of the mean, not just at the point. A naive guard that returns the normal tail there drops the third-cumulant (skewness) term and, over the band where the raw formula is noisy, makes the estimated tail non-monotone in qq.

The fix replaces the term by its Taylor series in θ\theta near the mean, 1û−1ŵ=c0+c1θ+O(θ2),c0=−K‴(0)6K″(0)3/2,c1=5K‴(0)224K″(0)5/2−K⁗(0)8K″(0)3/2, \frac{1}{\hat u} - \frac{1}{\hat w} = c_0 + c_1 \theta + O(\theta^2), \quad c_0 = -\frac{K'''(0)}{6\,K''(0)^{3/2}}, \quad c_1 = \frac{5\,K'''(0)^2}{24\,K''(0)^{5/2}} - \frac{K''''(0)}{8\,K''(0)^{3/2}}, with the central cumulants K″(0)=2∑λk2K''(0) = 2\sum\lambda_k^2, K‴(0)=8∑λk3K'''(0) = 8\sum\lambda_k^3, K⁗(0)=48∑λk4K''''(0) = 48\sum\lambda_k^4. The leading term gives the Daniels (1987) limit P(Q≥E[Q])=12+ϕ(0)c0=12−K‴(0)/(62πK″(0)3/2)P(Q \ge E[Q]) = \tfrac12 + \phi(0)\,c_0 = \tfrac12 - K'''(0)/(6\sqrt{2\pi}\,K''(0)^{3/2}), which is below 1/21/2 for a right-skewed QQ. The series is used while |ŵ|<0.1|\hat w| < 0.1, where the raw difference is unreliable; the direct formula runs in the tails, where it is accurate. This region carries p≈0.5p \approx 0.5 and never affects a rejection decision, but the function is now monotone and skewness-aware there rather than flat.

5. M2: the exact permutation CGF for non-Gaussian dd

5.1 The obstacle

The Lugannani-Rice machine needs only the CGF of the scalar QQ, KQ(θ)=log⁡E[eθQ]K_Q(\theta) = \log E[e^{\theta Q}]. For Gaussian ee that CGF is closed form (Section 4). For the true, non-Gaussian permutation law of ee there is generally no closed form for KQK_Q, and supplying it is the entire problem. Every standard quadratic-form tail method (Imhof, Davies, Farebrother, Liu-Tang-Zhang, and the saddlepoint version Kuonen) reduces QQ to a weighted sum of chi-squares, which is a Gaussian-only fact; none of them applies to a non-Gaussian, lattice ee.

5.2 The Hubbard-Stratonovich identity

We do have the joint CGF of ee, Ke(s)=log⁡E[es′e]K_e(s) = \log E[e^{s'e}], in closed form: it is the elementary-symmetric permutation CGF evaluated on the scores projected onto ss. The Hubbard-Stratonovich identity converts the quadratic form into a Gaussian average of that linear CGF. For θ>0\theta > 0, eθ‖e‖2=EW∼N(0,Ir)[e2θW′e], e^{\theta \lVert e \rVert^2} = E_{W \sim N(0, I_r)}\!\left[\, e^{\sqrt{2\theta}\, W'e} \,\right], because EW[ea′W]=e‖a‖2/2E_W[e^{a'W}] = e^{\lVert a\rVert^2/2} with a=2θea = \sqrt{2\theta}\,e. Taking the expectation over ee inside (the dependence on ee is now linear) gives the moment generating function of QQ as an exact rr-dimensional Gaussian integral, MQ(θ)=EW∼N(0,Ir)[exp(Ke(2θW))],KQ(θ)=log⁡MQ(θ). M_Q(\theta) = E_{W \sim N(0, I_r)}\!\left[\, \exp\!\big(K_e(\sqrt{2\theta}\, W)\big) \,\right], \qquad K_Q(\theta) = \log M_Q(\theta). Because ee has finite (permutation) support, KeK_e grows at most linearly, the −‖W‖2/2-\lVert W\rVert^2/2 Gaussian weight dominates, and the integral converges for all θ\theta. The bounded support also means QQ is bounded, so KQK_Q is entire: it has no pole, unlike the Gaussian weighted-chi-square CGF.

5.3 Why Laplace fails and quadrature succeeds

A natural first idea is to evaluate the Gaussian integral by Laplace’s method (steepest descent on WW). It does not work, for an instructive reason. The CGF KeK_e is centred, so ∇Ke(0)=0\nabla K_e(0) = 0 and W=0W = 0 is always the critical point; the leading-order Laplace expansion there returns exactly the Gaussian KQK_Q and discards all of the non-normality. The non-Gaussian content lives in the full integral, not in its mode. (The same fact has a clean reading through Kolassa-Robinson, below: a steepest-descent evaluation re-imposes a degenerate surface approximation; doing the angular integral exactly is what keeps the non-normality.)

The fix is to evaluate the Gaussian average by Gauss-Hermite quadrature – the standard rule for a Gaussian expectation – rather than by Laplace. With a tensor product of one-dimensional Gauss-Hermite nodes mapped to the N(0,Ir)N(0, I_r) measure, KQ(θ)=log⁡∑keℓkexp⁡(Ke(2θzk)), K_Q(\theta) = \log \sum_k e^{\,\ell_k}\, \exp\!\big(K_e(\sqrt{2\theta}\, z_k)\big), with nodes zkz_k and log-weights ℓk\ell_k. This recovers the exact KQK_Q: against full enumeration of the orbit, the Gauss-Hermite value matches to about 10−1510^{-15} for moderate θ\theta and to about 10−610^{-6} in the deep tail.

5.4 Inversion, derivatives, and the higher-order option

With KQK_Q in hand the inversion is the same Lugannani-Rice as M1. Because the Gauss-Hermite KQK_Q is accurate to near machine precision, its θ\theta-derivatives KQ′K_Q' and KQ″K_Q'' are taken by finite differences – no analytic gradient or Hessian of KeK_e is needed. The saddlepoint θ̂\hat\theta solves KQ′(θ̂)=qK_Q'(\hat\theta) = q; since QQ is bounded there is no pole to bracket against, and KQ′K_Q' maps θ\theta to the support range of QQ.

Alongside the Lugannani-Rice tail, M2 returns the Barndorff-Nielsen r*r^* refinement, P(Q≥q)≈1−Φ(ŵ+1ŵlogûŵ), P(Q \ge q) \approx 1 - \Phi\!\left(\hat w + \frac{1}{\hat w}\log\frac{\hat u}{\hat w}\right), which upgrades the relative error from O(n−1)O(n^{-1}) to O(n−3/2)O(n^{-3/2}) from the same ŵ,û\hat w, \hat u. This is the one place a higher-order asymptotic enters the pipeline; everything before it (the identity, the quadrature) is exact or numerically exact.

5.5 Robustness and the dimension limit

M2 is built to return a finite, sensible number in every case. Below E[Q]E[Q], where the upper-tail saddlepoint would need θ<0\theta < 0 (outside the Hubbard-Stratonovich range), it returns the Gaussian-dd tail, which is accurate there and not a rejection region. At the support edge or on a coarse lattice, where the finite-difference second derivative goes unreliable, it again falls back to the Gaussian tail with a warning rather than returning NaN or erroring.

The cost of the tensor Gauss-Hermite rule is nodesr\text{nodes}^r, so it is feasible only for small rr. At the default 32 nodes the function refuses r≥4r \ge 4 with an error that points at the unbuilt sparse-grid / quasi-Monte-Carlo engine (M3), which is the path to the many-covariate balance test rather than optional polish.

6. Where this sits in the literature

The nearest developed precedent is Kolassa and Robinson (2011), who give a saddlepoint treatment of a multivariate permutation test. They do not approximate the quadratic-form tail: they replace the quadratic form with a likelihood-ratio- like statistic, because the direct large-deviation tail of a quadratic form in a multivariate mean has relative error only O(n−1/4)O(n^{-1/4}) (Osipov, 1981), and they sidestep that barrier by changing the statistic. Their own table shows the classical Mahalanobis D2D^2 tail calibrated by chi-square is badly off in the tail, and they state accurate tails for it are “not available.” That classical D2D^2 is exactly the statistic RItools and Hansen-Bowers report, and the cell M2 fills.

The O(n−1/4)O(n^{-1/4}) barrier is a property of the method, not of the statistic: it comes from integrating a multivariate Edgeworth correction over a curved (ellipsoidal) level set, where the surface contribution carries an extra factor of n1/2n^{1/2} (Robinson, Hoglund, Holst and Quine, 1990, Corollary 2.1). M2 never forms that surface integral; the Hubbard-Stratonovich average runs over all directions of WW, which is the angular integration over the degenerate sphere of dominating points, and Gauss-Hermite does it exactly. So the curvature is folded exactly into the scalar KQK_Q and the barrier does not arise.

Two honest caveats temper any rate claim, and we have now tested both. First, escaping the curvature artifact is not the same as proving scalar O(1/n)O(1/n): the residual question is the discreteness of QQ at small stratum counts, not curvature. Second, the honest competitor is Imhof, not Osipov’s method; as the stratum count grows the inner Laplace becomes exact and Imhof is itself O(1/B)O(1/B), so M2’s gain over Imhof is a better constant at small BB – carrying the true skewness and kurtosis – not a better rate.

The decisive check is an experiment: the relative error of M2 against the exact permutation tail as the stratum count BB grows. We ran it (matched triples, skewed dd, metric VdV_d, full 3B3^B enumeration, tail depth p=0.05p = 0.05, averaged over random designs), and it confirms the second caveat against the first reading. M2’s relative error does not fall like 1/B1/B. It sits at 3 to 7 percent over B=8B = 8 to 1212 and, if anything, grows toward a floor, while the crude chi-square M1 keeps falling toward its own +0.5%+0.5\% limit. So the simulation revises the optimistic reading into the better-constant claim: M2 cuts the M1 p-value error 4- to 10-fold at the stratum counts a balance test uses (escaping the useless Osipov-rate D2D^2 tail), but it does not buy a better asymptotic rate.

The residual is a finite-discrete-representation effect, and a chain of controls rules out the obvious corrections. It is not a pipeline artifact: the Gauss-Hermite CGF reproduces the exact orbit CGF to 10−1410^{-14} at the saddle, so the gap is genuine Lugannani-Rice error inverting the exact CGF of a finite support. It is not the continuous saddlepoint: the analytic chi-square LR error is +0.5%+0.5\% for r=1,2,3r = 1, 2, 3 alike. It is not curvature: the bias falls with dimension – +15%+15\% at r=1r = 1, +7%+7\% at r=2r = 2, +2%+2\% at r=3r = 3 – where a count of discrete points against the curved level set would grow with rr. And it is not generic permutation discreteness: the scalar sum saddlepoint on the same orbit is accurate to under one percent. What remains is the gap between continuous Lugannani-Rice and the exact tail of a finite, discrete representation of QQ; a uniform law on nn i.i.d. exact chi-square draws shows the same bias against an analytic LR error of +0.5%+0.5\%. The practical reading is favorable: the Mahalanobis omnibus is used at r≥2r \ge 2 (a single covariate is a scalar test), the bias there is small and falls as covariates are added, and it is conservative – M2 reports p-values slightly too large. The full chain of experiments is in dev/route-b-rate-experiment-findings.md; a fuller literature discussion is in dev/route-b-literature.md.

On higher-order asymptotics specifically: the scalar r*r^* of Section 5.4 is the tail refinement of a statistic with a known CGF (Barndorff-Nielsen 1986; Brazzale, Davison and Reid 2007 is the practical reference). It is distinct from Brazzale’s core program, the r*r^* for a parameter of interest in a parametric likelihood with nuisance parameters, which our randomization null – no likelihood, no nuisance parameter – does not invoke.

7. Known limitation: coarse lattices and the finite-discrete residual

M2 is much more accurate than M1 on the dense, multi-stratum support balance testing has – 4 to 10 times better in the rate experiment of Section 6 – but it carries the finite-discrete residual diagnosed there, and a separate coarse-lattice edge case. On a single or double stratum VdV_d is proportional to the sample covariance of the scores (so the metric choices coincide), and QQ’s support is a coarse, atom-heavy lattice; the continuous saddlepoint then under- or overshoots the discrete tail, so M2 falls back to the Gaussian tail there. That fallback ships.

The dense-support residual (Section 6) is not addressed by a continuity correction, and we are explicit that we do not implement one: the controls show it is not a regular lattice (no fixed span; the local span shrinks like 1/N1/N, which would predict a vanishing bias the data contradict), not the empirical CGF’s tail-max, not boundary curvature, and not the continuous chi-square saddlepoint. It is the gap between continuous Lugannani-Rice and the exact tail of a finite, discrete QQ, and it shrinks with dimension rather than growing. Because that residual is small and falling at the r≥2r \ge 2 where the omnibus is used, conservative in sign, and already far below M1, a finite-discrete correction (an Euler-Maclaurin-type boundary term) is research-level work whose payoff we judge not worth its complexity for this application. The path forward is to wire M2 into the balance-test front ends, not to chase the last few percent at low rr.

8. Validation

Every claim above is checked against the exact permutation distribution, obtained by walking the entire within-stratum orbit (no Monte Carlo error) for the small designs the tests use. The oracle is enumerate_Q in the test helper. On a dense ten-pair orbit with skewed scores and M=ΣxM = \Sigma_x, M2 tracks the exact tail to within 3 to 5 percent where the Gaussian M1 is off by 15 to 340 percent – the gap widens with the skewness of ee, as the theory predicts.

library(fastperm)
# eight matched pairs; the second covariate is skewed (fibonacci), so the
# permutation law of Q is non-normal and the Gaussian tail drifts
scores <- cbind(rep(c(1, 2), 8) + rep(0:7, each = 2) * 0.4,
                c(rbind(rep(1, 8), c(2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55))))
strata <- rep(1:8, each = 2)
# treat the high-score unit in five of the eight pairs (a moderate imbalance)
z <- rep(0, 16)
for (b in 1:8) z[if (b <= 5) 2 * b else 2 * b - 1] <- 1
# Gaussian (M1) versus the non-normal permutation saddlepoint (M2)
fastperm_spa_quadratic(scores, z, strata, method = "gaussian")$p.value
#> [1] 0.05205406
res <- fastperm_spa_quadratic(scores, z, strata, method = "saddlepoint")
c(lugannani_rice = res$p.value, r_star = res$p.value.rstar)
#> lugannani_rice         r_star 
#>     0.02712069     0.02712045

9. Decisions, with code and test locations

Each row is a decision, the function that implements it (in R/saddlepoint-quadratic.R unless noted), and the test that guards it (in tests/testthat/test-saddlepoint-quadratic.R unless noted).

  • Rotation reduction Q=‖R′(T−μ)‖2Q = \lVert R'(T-\mu)\rVert^2, metric as preprocessing. .quad_inv_sqrt (the M−1/2M^{-1/2} rotation). Test: “the rotation reduction Q=‖dy‖2Q = \lVert d_y\rVert^2 is an exact identity”.
  • Metric as a caller-supplied parameter (“cov” or a matrix). fastperm_spa_quadratic argument metric. Tests: “M1 with metric = ‘cov’ reduces to the chi-square tail”; “M1 reproduces imhof for a non-identity metric”.
  • Exact permutation mean and covariance (Strasser-Weber). fastperm_linear_cgf_mv in R/cgf-stratified-mv.R. Test: “the enabler’s permutation covariance matches the orbit covariance”.
  • M1 Lugannani-Rice on the weighted-chi-square CGF. .quad_lr_upper. Tests: “M1 with metric = ‘cov’ reduces to the chi-square tail”; “M1 reproduces imhof for a non-identity metric”.
  • M1 near-mean Daniels limit and Taylor series (the cancellation fix). .quad_lr_upper (coefficients c0, c1). Tests: “.quad_lr_upper returns the Daniels skewness limit at the mean, not 1/2”; “.quad_lr_upper is continuous and monotone across the mean”.
  • M2 Hubbard-Stratonovich CGF by Gauss-Hermite quadrature. .make_KQ_quad, .tensor_normal, .gh_nodes. The Laplace dead-end and the quadrature fix are recorded in dev/route-b-quadratic-inversion.md.
  • Vectorised multi-node elementary-symmetric evaluation (the speedup). .log_esym_cols (a column-vectorised .log_esym from R/cgf-stratified.R).
  • M2 finite-difference θ\theta-derivatives (justified by machine-precision GH). .quad_spa_upper.
  • M2 Lugannani-Rice tail plus Barndorff-Nielsen r*r^*. .quad_spa_upper (returned as p.value and p.value.rstar). Test: “M2 (saddlepoint) returns a finite tail and a Barndorff-Nielsen r*“.
  • M2 Gaussian fallback below E[Q]E[Q], at the support edge, and on coarse lattices. .quad_spa_upper. Test: “M2 is never worse than M1 against the exact tail at the observed Q”.
  • M2 accuracy and improvement over M1 on the skewed dense case. Test: “M2 matches the exact permutation tail and beats M1 where d is skewed”.
  • Tensor-grid dimension guard pointing at M3. fastperm_spa_quadratic (the nodes^r > 250000 check). Test: “M2 errors for rank too large for the tensor grid, pointing past M2”.
  • Exact-enumeration oracle (ground truth for all of the above). enumerate_Q, enum_quadratic_tail in tests/testthat/helper-quadratic-enumerate.R.
